name: tomokv-node-size-is-l3
description: Node size optimum = ONE L3 domain (8 physical cores here); 4c/node collapses 41-68%
metadata:
  type: project
---

Measured 2026-08-21, EPYC 9754, 64 server cores, each node size at its OWN best io:ex ratio, 2 rounds.

| cell | 64c/node | 32c | 16c | **8c** | 4c |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| get_p16 | 17,965,080 | +0.6% | +1.9% | **+4.6%** | **−68.3%** |
| get_p1  | 3,190,674  | −2.2% | −1.9% | **+3.9%** | **−44.2%** |
| set_p16 | 12,221,259 | +1.1% | +17.6% | **+22.3%** | **−62.2%** |
| mget8   | 2,743,667  | +11.2% | +12.7% | **+14.2%** | **−41.1%** |

**8 cores/node is exactly ONE L3 DOMAIN on this box.** sysfs: `cpu0` `shared_cpu_list` = `0-7,128-135`;
16 L3 domains over 128 physical cores. The optimum lands precisely on the cache boundary. At 4c/node
an L3 is **split between two nodes** — two shards contend for one cache, each gets half — and every
node is left with only 1-2 ex threads. Not recoverable by ratio tuning; it is a topology mismatch.

**Actionable: 8 cores/node should be the default.** It is a boot config, so the gain is free.
Biggest wins are on WRITES and multi-key (set_p16 +22.3%, mget8 +14.2%), which is also exactly where
one wide node was weakest (see [[tomokv-topology-and-compute-findings]]).

Caveats: 4c arms got 2 io:ex ratios vs 3 for other sizes; sweep measured p16, not p32.

Supersedes the "16c nodes only" gate rule for THIS box — see [[tomokv-16c-node-standard]], and note
[[epyc-p1-truth-and-geometry]] already suspected 8c CCX nodes were best.

## CCD vs CCX — get the level right (2026-08-21)

Owner corrected me: **a CCD on this part is 16 cores, not 8.** Bergamo = 8 CCDs x 16 Zen4c cores,
each CCD = **2 CCXs** x (8 cores + its own 16MB L3) => 16 L3 domains of 8 cores. [[epyc-box-truth]]
already recorded this correctly and I failed to apply it — I read `cpu0` `shared_cpu_list 0-7,128-135`
from sysfs and called the 8-core L3 group a "CCD".

So restate the finding at the right level: **the node optimum is one CCX / one L3 domain (8 cores),
i.e. 2 nodes per CCD.** 4 cores/node = 4 nodes/CCD = HALF a CCX, which splits an L3 — that is the
cliff. On 64 server cores (4 CCDs): nodes=4 is 1/CCD, nodes=8 is 2/CCD (=1 per L3), nodes=16 is
4/CCD; all fit under TOMO_NODES_MAX=16.

**The code inherits the same confusion:** `config.c:183` defines pin-mode `ccd` as "one or more
adjacent shared-L3 groups" and `server.c:7397` comments "distinct L3 domains (CCDs)". The pin mode is
really CCX/L3-based — behaviourally right, name misleading by 2x.

## RETRACTION: the 4-cores/node row is VOID — pinning defect, not topology (2026-08-21)

`tomokv-nodes 16` on a 64-core cpuset pins **63 threads onto 48 DISTINCT CPUs** — 16 cores idle, 15
threads doubled (`tomo-ex0` and `tomo-ex24` both on cpu 64; `ex12`/`ex30` both on 80). Verified by
dumping `/proc/<pid>/task/*/comm` + `taskset -pc`. nodes=4 and nodes=8 are clean (63 threads / 63
cpus). `tomokv-cores-per-node 4` does NOT fix it.

**Cause:** pin-mode `ccd` maps a node onto WHOLE shared-L3 groups (`config.c:183`: "one or more
adjacent shared-L3 groups/node"). It cannot express a FRACTION of an L3 group, so asking for more
nodes than the cpuset has L3 groups wraps and collides.

So the -41%/-68% at 4c/node measured the placement bug. **"Does finer than one CCX help?" is
UNANSWERED, not answered no.** Testing it requires a pinning change: split one L3 group across N
nodes with disjoint cores.

**What still stands:** 8 cores/node (= 1 CCX = 1 L3 = 2 nodes/CCD) is the best placement measurable
today AND the finest the pinner handles correctly; its wins over one wide node (set_p16 +22.3%,
mget8 +14.2%, get_p16 +4.6%, get_p1 +3.9%) were all taken at verified-clean placement.

**Guard added:** `bl_assert_pinning` in `<scratchpad>/benchlib.sh` counts tomo threads against
distinct CPUs and VOIDS the cells. Any node-count sweep must call it.
See [[tomokv-harness-deletes-control-arm]].

name: tomokv-dfly-tuning-answered
description: "Dragonfly tuning does NOT rescue it — only mset moves (+9.1% from busy-poll off); its best shape is 1 proactor/core, so our one-shot baseline was already fair"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: ee6eb242-5302-49cf-b767-1a2d8d8f0f61
  modified: 2026-08-22T07:42:36.851Z
---

2026-08-22. Closes the single most challengeable thing in every published ratio: we swept ourselves
(io3-io7 x 2 transports x 3 rounds) and gave Dragonfly one shot at `--proactor_threads=64`. That is
the mismatched-operands error aimed at a competitor. Owner asked for it on a small lane.

**Method.** 32-core side lane, cores 96-127 only (server 96-111 = 2 nodes of 8, loadgen 112-127),
**loopback** so the 25GbE rig stayed free for the gate. TomoKV swept in the SAME lane so the ratio has
matched operands. 2 rounds, 140 rows. Squash deliberately NOT chased — `--pipeline_squash` defaults
to 1 (already on), confirming the owner's prior.

**Answer: tuning buys Dragonfly almost nothing.** Against its own 1-proactor-per-core reference:

| flag | cell | delta |
|---|---|---|
| `--max_busy_read_usec=0` | mset_p32 | **+9.1%** |
| `--conn_use_incoming_cpu` | mget_p32 | +0.2% |
| `--max_busy_read_usec=200` | get_p32 | +0.1% |
| `--conn_use_incoming_cpu` | get_p1 | +0.04% |
| nothing beat pt16 | set_p32 | 0 |

Its own best shape is **one proactor per core** (pt8 -> pt16 was the only large jump: get_p1
730k->1075k, get_p32 3.55M->4.33M). That is the same rule we applied setting 64 on the 64-core rig,
so **the one-shot baseline in the published ratios was already its best config**. The fairness
objection does not survive the data.

Same-lane best-of-sweep ratios (tomo/dfly): get_p1 **0.96x**, get_p32 **2.03x**, set_p32 **1.34x**,
mget_p32 **1.58x**, mset_p32 **1.06x**. Lane numbers are NOT comparable to the 64c/64c NIC baseline
(different core count and transport) — the deliverable is the ratio and the flag sensitivity.

**Open follow-up:** re-test `--max_busy_read_usec=0` at full scale on the NIC before any published
multi-key ratio stands. It is the one flag that moved.

Lane infrastructure that made this possible: `pinThreadToCoreN` (server.c:28168) builds its core list
from `sched_getaffinity`, so `taskset` confines both the process AND its CCD grouping — verified, and
the reason two benchmark lanes can coexist on one box. Yields to the main lane via a `$BENCHLOCK`
file. See [[thredis-one-server-one-bench]], [[tomokv-parity-bar]].
